title: DO NOT DESPISE SMALL BEGINNINGS
paragraphs: DO NOT DESPISE SMALL BEGINNINGS
Understanding the Deep Meaning of Zechariah 4:10
Some of the greatest works of God begin so small that human eyes almost miss them.
A shepherd boy standing alone in a field.
A widow with a handful of flour.
A teenage girl in Nazareth.
A carpenter from Galilee.
Twelve ordinary disciples.
A cross on a hill.
A borrowed tomb.
And perhaps right now, a weary believer reading these words wondering if their life matters at all.

The tragedy of the human heart is that we often measure significance by size. We celebrate crowds, numbers, influence, applause, and visible success. We assume that if God is moving, it must look impressive. If God is blessing, it must look large. If God is working, surely everyone will notice.
Yet Scripture repeatedly reveals a God who delights in beginnings so small they appear insignificant to everyone except Him.
This truth explodes from one of the most powerful statements in the Old Testament:

“For who hath despised the day of small things?”
(Zechariah 4:10)
Many believers quote this verse. Few fully understand the depth behind it.
To understand its meaning, we must first step into the dust, disappointment, and discouragement of a people trying to rebuild what seemed impossible.
Jerusalem lay in ruins.

The glorious Temple of Solomon had been destroyed by Babylon decades earlier. The people had experienced exile, judgment, humiliation, and loss. Everything that once symbolized national strength and covenant blessing appeared shattered.
Then God brought a remnant home.
The people returned to Jerusalem with hope.
But hope quickly collided with reality.
The city was devastated.
Resources were limited.
Opposition was constant.
The new Temple foundation looked embarrassingly small compared to Solomon’s magnificent structure.
Many older Jews who remembered the former Temple wept when they saw the new foundation.
It seemed insignificant.
It seemed weak.
It seemed disappointing.
It seemed like failure.
And that is precisely where God spoke.
The Hebrew text reads:
כִּי מִי בַז לְיוֹם קְטַנּוֹת
Ki mi vaz le-yom qetannot?
Literally:
“For who has despised the day of small things?”
The word “בַז” (baz) means to scorn, despise, treat with contempt, or consider worthless.
The word “קְטַנּוֹת” (qetannot) refers to things that are small, insignificant, seemingly unimportant, or lacking visible greatness.
God was confronting a dangerous attitude.
The problem was not the size of the work.
The problem was the perspective of the people.
They were evaluating God's work through human expectations.
They saw a tiny foundation.
God saw a future Temple.
They saw weakness.
God saw faithfulness.
They saw limitations.
God saw His sovereign plan unfolding.
This is why Zechariah 4 begins with one of the most famous declarations in Scripture:

“Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.”
(Zechariah 4:6)
The Hebrew reads:
לֹא בְחַיִל וְלֹא בְכֹחַ כִּי אִם־בְּרוּחִי
Lo bechayil velo bekoach ki im beruchi
“Not by military strength, not by human power, but by My Spirit.”
God was teaching His people a lesson that echoes through every generation.
The Kingdom of God does not advance through human impressiveness.
It advances through divine faithfulness.
That truth reaches its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
When the Messiah arrived, He came in a way nobody expected.
No royal palace.
No military army.
No political throne.
No worldly prestige.
The prophet Isaiah described Him this way:

“He hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him.”
(Isaiah 53:2)
To many people, Jesus looked ordinary.
To some, He looked insignificant.
To others, He looked like a failure.
Then came the scandal of the cross.
The Roman execution stake became history’s greatest paradox.
What appeared to be defeat became victory.
What looked like weakness became power.
What seemed like an ending became a beginning.
The Greek word used throughout the New Testament for the Gospel is εὐαγγέλιον (euangelion), meaning “good news.”
The greatest news in human history began with what looked like catastrophe.
The disciples saw death.
God saw redemption.
The world saw shame.
God saw salvation.
Hell celebrated too early.
Sunday morning was coming.
The resurrection itself is proof that God specializes in transforming small beginnings into eternal victories.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
This is the heartbeat of Zechariah 4:10.
This is the heartbeat of our theme:
Maybe your faith feels small right now.
Maybe your prayers seem unanswered.
Maybe your ministry feels unnoticed.
Maybe your obedience feels insignificant.
Maybe your family restoration has only begun.
Maybe your healing has only taken its first step.
Maybe your repentance feels fragile.
Maybe your spiritual growth feels painfully slow.
The world says small means unimportant.
God says small can become sacred.
Jesus Himself taught:

“The kingdom of heaven is like to a grain of mustard seed.”
(Matthew 13:31)
The mustard seed was famous for its tiny size.
Yet Christ used it as an illustration of explosive Kingdom growth.
God often begins with what people overlook.
A prayer whispered through tears.
A Bible opened after years away.
A confession finally spoken.
A broken heart finally surrendered.
A single act of obedience.
A small beginning.
Never underestimate what God can do with one surrendered life.
The enemy wants believers discouraged because the work seems unfinished.
God rejoices because the work has begun.
Notice the second half of Zechariah 4:10:
“For they shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel.”
The people were focused on what was incomplete.
God celebrated progress.
The Lord rejoiced not merely at the completed Temple but at the evidence that His purposes were moving forward.
This reveals something beautiful about God's character.
He is not only the God of completion.
He is also the God of beginnings.
He celebrates every genuine step toward Him.
Every prayer.
Every act of repentance.
Every sacrifice.
Every effort to follow Christ.
Every battle fought against sin.
Every attempt to trust Him again.
He sees what others overlook.
He values what others dismiss.
He remembers what others forget.
Perhaps that is why Jesus said in Matthew 10:42 that even a cup of cold water given in His name will not lose its reward.
Nothing done for Christ is insignificant.
Nothing surrendered to Christ is wasted.
Nothing entrusted to Christ is forgotten.
And perhaps someone reading this needed that reminder today.
Because you have been judging your life by visible results.
God is measuring it by faithfulness.
You have been counting crowds.
God has been counting obedience.
You have been staring at unfinished walls.
God has been looking at the foundation He Himself laid.
The Gospel never promises instant transformation.
It promises certain transformation through Christ.
The same Jesus who began a good work in His people will complete it.
The apostle Paul wrote:

“He which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ.”
(Philippians 1:6)
Notice the language.
Began.
God is a God of beginnings.
The cross looked small.
The tomb looked final.
The church looked fragile.
Yet today billions know the name of Jesus Christ because God never despises small beginnings.
Neither should we.
They may need this encouragement more than you realize.
What small beginning are you trusting God with right now?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
The foundation you almost gave up on may be the very place where God is preparing His greatest testimony.
